passages.t: ‘Leave your country’: the call and the promise
passages.happening:
God speaks to Abram. “Leave your country, your kindred, and your father’s household, and go to the land I will show you” (verse 1). God does not say where the land is.

Then come the promises. “I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, so that you will be a blessing” (verse 2).

And the last promise reaches past Abram's family to the whole world: “I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
In Abram's world, your ‘father's household’ was your safety. It held the land, the flocks, the family graves and the family name. If someone harmed you, your family stood up for you. To leave it was to become an outsider, living by the goodwill of strangers. God asks Abram to give up three circles of belonging at once: his country, his relatives and his father's house.

Abram's family came from Ur and settled in Haran. Both cities worshiped the moon god. Joshua later says Abram's father “worshiped other gods” (Joshua 24:2). So God does not call a man who was already seeking him. He calls a man from a family of other gods.

The first hearers would also hear the story before this one. At Babel people said, ‘let us make a name for ourselves’ (11:4). Here God says, ‘I will make your name great’. The builders grabbed at a name. Abram is given one.

The word ‘bless’ comes five times in these three verses. In the chapters before, the word ‘curse’ kept coming back: on the serpent, on the ground, on Cain. Now God answers curse with blessing. And the word for ‘families’ in verse 3 is the word used in chapter 10 for the families of the nations. Every family that was scattered at Babel is named in this promise.
passages.later:
Paul calls this promise the good news told in advance. He writes that “The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham” (Galatians 3:8). Gentiles means people who are not Jewish. To justify means to count someone as right with God. Paul says that “those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith” (Galatians 3:9).

Peter preached the same promise in the temple: “Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed” (Acts 3:25).

Hebrews remembers the moment Abram left: he “obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going” (Hebrews 11:8). And Jesus says that “many will come from the east and the west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 8:11). The families of the earth end up at one table.
passages.hard:
Two questions come up in these verses.

First, the last line. The Hebrew can be read two ways. Most often it is read ‘all the families of the earth will be blessed through you’, as the BSB has it. The old Greek translation and the New Testament read it this way (Galatians 3:8; Acts 3:25). But when the promise comes back in 22:18 and 26:4, the verb has a slightly different form that more naturally means ‘will bless themselves by you’. That would mean the nations will use Abram's name when they pray for a blessing: ‘May God bless you as he blessed Abraham.’ Some translations use that wording. Both readings say the same big thing: God's choice of Abram is about the whole world.

That is why being chosen is not the same as being a favorite. God chooses one family so that he can bless all the others through it. In the Bible, being chosen is a task, not a trophy.

Second, ‘I will bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you’. This is God's promise to protect Abram and his family as he carries the blessing. Some Christians read this line as a guide for how nations today should treat the modern state of Israel. Others answer that it is a promise to Abram, not a rule for any government. These notes make no claim about any modern state, border or conflict. They read the line as Genesis gives it: God will stand with the family he has called, so that the blessing can reach everyone. In the Hebrew the ones who bless are many and the one who curses is one, which many readers take to mean that blessing is meant to be the rule.
passages.asks: Abram was called to leave what made him feel safe, without being told where he was going. Ask what you hold onto for safety. Then ask a second question: if God has blessed you, who is that blessing meant to reach through you?

passages.t: Abram goes, and the land is promised
passages.happening:
“So Abram departed, as the LORD had directed him, and Lot went with him” (verse 4). Abram is seventy-five years old. He takes his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, their goods and their servants, and sets out for Canaan (verse 5).

He travels as far as the Oak of Moreh at Shechem. The text adds, “And at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (verse 6).

Then the LORD appears to him and says, “I will give this land to your offspring.” Abram builds an altar there (verse 7). He moves on to the hills near Bethel, builds another altar, and “called on the name of the LORD” (verse 8). Then he keeps moving south toward the Negev (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Notice that the land is not empty. The Canaanites already live there. Abram arrives as a guest in other people's country. He owns no field. He lives in a tent and keeps moving.

Offspring means children and grandchildren and all the generations after. God promises the land to Abram's offspring, not to Abram himself. And Abram and Sarai have no children (11:30). The promise starts with a problem only God can solve.

The places matter. Shechem and Bethel later become important places of worship in Israel. Joshua gathers the people at Shechem to renew their promise to serve the LORD (Joshua 24:1). Great trees were often places where people looked for guidance from their gods. Abram builds altars to the LORD there instead. Each altar says: this land belongs to the LORD.

The Negev is the dry country in the far south. It is the first place to suffer when the winter rains fail. That sets up what happens next.
passages.later:
Stephen tells the story in Acts: God gave Abraham “no inheritance here, not even a foot of ground. But God promised to give possession of the land to Abraham and his descendants, even though he did not yet have a child” (Acts 7:5).

Hebrews says Abraham “dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents” (Hebrews 11:9). And it says what he was hoping for: “they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16).

Paul goes further. He speaks of “the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world” (Romans 4:13). Jesus says, “Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).
passages.hard:
What does God promise here, and who receives it today?

First, what the text says. God promises this land, Canaan, to Abram's offspring (verse 7). Later he says ‘forever’ (13:15) and gives wide borders (15:18). Abram himself never owns any of it except a grave he buys for Sarah (chapter 23). Israel's law later says the land always belonged to God: “The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine” (Leviticus 25:23).

Second, how the New Testament takes it up. Hebrews says Abraham was looking for “a better country, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16). Paul calls Abraham “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13). The promise of one land opens out toward a whole renewed earth.

Christians read the land promise in more than one way. Some hold that the promise still belongs to the Jewish people and that God will keep it in history, because “God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29). Others hold that in Christ the promise widens to the whole earth, inherited by all who belong to him (Galatians 3:29). Many hold something of both. These notes take no side.

These notes make no claim about any modern state, border or conflict. Nothing here is said against any people, ancient or modern: not the Canaanites, not the Jewish people, not the Arab peoples, not anyone who lives in that land today. On every reading the land was God's gift, never something earned or seized.
passages.asks: Abram lived in tents in a land that was promised but not yet his. Ask what promise of God you are still waiting on. Then ask what it would look like to build an altar where you are now: to worship before you see the promise kept.

passages.happening:
A famine strikes, and Abram goes down to Egypt (verse 10). On the way he says to Sarai, “Look, I know that you are a beautiful woman, and when the Egyptians see you, they will say, ‘This is his wife.’ Then they will kill me but will let you live” (verses 11-12). So he asks her to say she is his sister (verse 13).

Pharaoh's officials see Sarai, praise her to Pharaoh, and “she was taken into the palace of Pharaoh” (verse 15). Abram is given sheep, cattle, donkeys, servants and camels (verse 16).

Then “The LORD, however, afflicted Pharaoh and his household with severe plagues because of Abram’s wife Sarai” (verse 17). Pharaoh calls Abram: “What have you done to me? Why didn’t you tell me she was your wife?” (verse 18). He gives Sarai back and sends them away (verses 19-20).
passages.hearers:
When the rain failed in Canaan, Egypt was the place to go. Egypt did not depend on rain. It depended on the Nile, which flooded every year and watered the fields. A painting in an Egyptian official's tomb at Beni Hasan, from the 1800s BC, shows a group of people from western Asia arriving in Egypt with their donkeys, women and children. Herders like Abram really did come.

‘Pharaoh’ is not a name. It comes from an Egyptian phrase meaning ‘great house’. At first it meant the king's palace. Later it came to mean the king himself, the way people say ‘the White House’ when they mean the president. Genesis never names this Pharaoh.

Sarai really was Abram's half-sister: the daughter of his father but not of his mother (20:12). So what he told her to say was half true. A half-truth told to deceive is still a lie.

The camels in verse 16 are debated. A 2013 study by Tel Aviv University found that tame camels became common in that region only in the late 900s BC. Some take the camels as told in the terms of a later age. Others reply that camels were rare but known earlier.

The first hearers would also notice a pattern. A famine brings the family down to Egypt. Pharaoh takes what is not his. The LORD strikes his house with plagues. Pharaoh sends them away with great wealth. It is the exodus story in small, long before the exodus.
passages.later:
Genesis tells this kind of story three times. Abraham does it again with Abimelech (Genesis 20), and his son Isaac does the same thing with his own wife (Genesis 26). Fear runs in families.

A psalm looks back on these years: “He let no man oppress them; He rebuked kings on their behalf” (Psalm 105:14).

The pattern of famine, Egypt, plagues and release comes back at full size in Exodus, when God strikes Egypt and Israel leaves with much wealth (Exodus 12:35-36).

Hebrews 11 remembers Abraham's faith, not this failure. But Genesis does not hide it. The Bible's heroes are not shown as perfect, and the promise is kept because God keeps it.
passages.hard:
This is a story about a man who put his wife in danger to save himself.

The text does not excuse him. Abram speaks about his own life: ‘they will kill me’. He says nothing about what will happen to Sarai. She never speaks in the whole story. Things are done to her: she is seen, praised and taken. Abram comes out richer. The one who tells the truth is Pharaoh, the outsider. He asks the man of God, ‘What have you done to me?’ and Abram has no answer.

Some old readers tried to defend Abram, saying that she was his sister after all. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, old and new, say plainly that what he did was wrong. The way Genesis tells the story agrees with them.

Who does God act for? Sarai. The plagues come “because of Abram’s wife Sarai” (verse 17). God steps in to protect the woman her husband would not protect.

A word for anyone who has been put at risk by someone who should have protected you: a parent, a husband or wife, a leader. This story does not call that faith. The Bible names it, and so should we. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The God of this chapter acts for Sarai. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Abram trusted God enough to leave home, then trusted his own plan the moment he felt afraid. Ask where fear makes you protect yourself at someone else's cost. Then ask who in your life is counting on you to protect them, not to use them.
